title: Cross-environment audit egress orchestration with opaque manifest protocol
creator: Asha Patel
description:
Problem: Customers deploying Redwood Private / VPC / on-prem require reliable, auditable forwarding of platform audit events to customer-managed storage (S3/GCS/Blob) while preserving security controls (CMEK, signed manifests, resumable uploads) and operational guarantees across network-constrained environments. Current forwarders are brittle across air-gapped/egress-restricted setups and lack a compact, forward-compatible handoff protocol for verifying completeness and ordering without leaking sensitive metadata.

Goal: Design and implement an orchestration layer and protocol (opaque manifest protocol) for audit egress that: 1) supports resumable chunked uploads to customer bucket endpoints, 2) exposes a deterministic manifest that proves a contiguous sequence of events, 3) provides atomic handoff semantics across private/VPC/on-prem network constraints, 4) integrates with RBAC v2 and SSO admin controls for granting egress permissions, and 5) supports fallback to internal sinks or escrow when uploads fail or CMEK handshake cannot complete.
acceptance_criteria: Forwarder can produce signed opaque manifests that enumerate committed segments (by sequence range) and a cryptographic checksum; manifests are uploaded to customer storage and verifiable by Redwood admin tools without exposing plaintext event contents.

Resumable uploads: large audit archives sliced into chunk uploads (multipart) with server- and client-side resume semantics; partial uploads recoverable after network interruptions without duplication or sequence gaps.

CMEK handshake: when customer requests CMEK, forwarder supports envelope key wrap and an explicit CMEK handshake flow with retries and clear operator-visible errors; inability to complete CMEK results in configurable policy: fail, escrow, or use platform-managed keys depending on tenant config.

Admin control integration: SSO/SAML-enabled admin roles can grant and revoke egress destinations; RBAC v2 rules enforce which operator/service accounts can create egress connectors and rotate signing keys.

Fallback behaviour: on sustained upload failures (configurable threshold), events are retained and routed to an escrow sink with operator notification; canary rollouts validate manifest semantics on a small tenant subset before broad rollout.
Observability: metrics emitted for per-tenant egress success/failure, upload latency, manifest verification time, and bytes committed; dashboards and alerts added to Console release-2026.03.
proposed_design:
We propose adding an orchestration component (audit-egress-orchestrator) that sits inside the Private control plane and exposes a single outbound egress worker per region. The worker performs three responsibilities: chunked upload engine, manifest manager, and handoff coordinator.

Opaque manifest protocol: the manifest is a compact JSON-LD-like structure (but not exposing event payloads) containing: tenant_id, manifest_id (UUID), start_seq, end_seq, list of segment entries (segment_id, offset_start, offset_end, encrypted_chunk_sha256), signing_key_id, signed_blob (Ed25519 signature of canonicalized manifest). The manifest proves contiguous coverage of a sequence range and lists chunk checksums so receivers can verify integrity without server-side decode. The manifest itself is encrypted and signed depending on customer policy.

Upload flow: 1) Worker aggregates events into a segment, encrypts with envelope key, slices into N multipart chunks. 2) Chunks uploaded in parallel to customer endpoint (S3/compatible/GCS) using presigned URLs or customer-provided credentials. 3) After successful chunk commits, worker writes manifest to a "manifests/" path with atomic rename (where supported) or an append-index file that records manifest id. 4) Worker acknowledges earliest commit to local ledger and purges KV cache once manifest confirmation observed (configurable retention window).

Airgap/relay mode: For on-prem air-gapped installs, the worker can write encrypted bundles to a local escrow directory and expose a signed manifest for offline transfer (tape/shuttle). A small signature header lets Redwood (or operator) verify completeness when imported into customer cloud.

RBAC and SSO integration: Egress connectors are CR-like objects controlled by RBAC v2 policies. Only roles with egress.create/egress.update can provision connectors; SSO group mappings permit admin-only rotation of signing keys and CMEK policy changes. All egress operations create audit entries in the internal control plane (separate from tenant audit streams) and require two-person approval for high-risk operations (e.g., change of destination bucket).
implementation_notes:
Phased implementation: Phase 1: implement manifest manager and chunked uploader for S3-compatible endpoints; integrate with existing audit-forwarder codepath and add unit/integration tests. Phase 2: CMEK handshake flow and policy flags; operator UI for egress connector lifecycle in Console. Phase 3: Airgap/escrow export/import tooling and offline manifest verification CLI. Phase 4: RBAC v2 policy checks and SSO/SAML admin workflows with approval flows.

Key modules: orchestrator service (Go), chunk upload client (reusable library), manifest signer (Ed25519), local ledger (SQLite for Private deployments), console UI + API surface for connector lifecycle. Use existing storage-adapter interfaces to reuse S3/GCS/Azure code.

Backward compatibility: Provide translation shim that accepts existing forwarder manifests and emits opaque manifests with equivalent sequence coverage to avoid reprocessing by customers.
risks: Complexity of guaranteeing atomicity across diverse storage providers (S3 vs GCS vs on-prem object stores) — different eventual consistency semantics could lead to false positives on manifest availability.
CMEK incomplete handshake may leave tenants in a suspended egress state; need clear operator remediation and automated retry/exp backoff policies.
Key management complexity: signing key rotation for manifests must be coordinated with customers if they verify signatures; improper rotation may break verification.
Performance/regressions: chunked uploads increase CPU and memory on private control plane; need resource limits and backpressure policies to avoid impacting serving runtime.
test_plan: Unit tests for manifest canonicalization and signature verification. Integration tests: end-to-end upload to S3 and MinIO (simulate eventual consistency), manifest verification by a verifier tool, CMEK handshake simulated with KMS emulator. Chaos tests: network partition during multipart upload and resume. Canary rollout: enable feature for 5 internal tenants and validate observability metrics, then 10 external beta tenants before full fleet rollout. Include regression tests that ensure no duplicate event writes and sequence monotonicity.
